title: Book 16 — Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus
paragraphs: Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd had lit a fire in the hut and were preparing breakfast at daybreak, having sent the men out with the pigs. When Telemachus arrived, the dogs didn’t bark but wagged their tails at him, so Odysseus, hearing footsteps and noticing that the dogs weren’t barking, said to Eumaeus:
“Eumaeus, I hear footsteps. I think one of your men or someone you know is coming here, because the dogs are wagging their tails at him and not barking.”

The words had barely left his mouth when his son appeared at the door. Eumaeus jumped to his feet, and the bowls he was using to mix wine fell from his hands as he rushed toward his master. He kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes, weeping with joy. A father couldn’t be more delighted at the return of an only son, a child of his old age, after ten years away in a foreign land and much suffering. He embraced him, kissed him all over as if he had returned from the dead, and spoke lovingly to him:

“So you’ve come, Telemachus, light of my eyes that you are. When I heard you’d gone to Pylos, I was sure I’d never see you again. Come in, dear boy, and sit down so I can get a good look at you now that you’re home. It’s not very often you come into the country to see us herdsmen—you usually stay close to town. I suppose you think it’s better to keep an eye on what the suitors are doing.”

“So be it, old friend,” Telemachus replied, “but I’ve come now because I want to see you and find out whether my mother is still in her old home, or if someone else has married her, leaving Odysseus’s bed without bedding and covered with cobwebs.”
“She’s still at the house,” Eumaeus answered, “grieving and heartbroken, doing nothing but weep both night and day, continually.”

As he spoke, he took Telemachus’s spear, and the young man crossed the stone threshold and entered. Odysseus rose from his seat to make room as he came in, but Telemachus stopped him. “Sit down, stranger,” he said. “I can easily find another seat, and someone here will prepare it for me.”

Odysseus returned to his place, and Eumaeus spread fresh brushwood on the floor and threw a sheepskin on top for Telemachus to sit on. Then the swineherd brought them plates of cold meat left over from the day before, and filled bread baskets as quickly as he could. He also mixed wine in bowls of ivy-wood and sat down facing Odysseus. They helped themselves to the good food before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said to Eumaeus, “Old friend, where does this stranger come from? How did his crew bring him to Ithaca, and who were they? He certainly didn’t come here by land.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “My son, I’ll tell you the real truth. He says he’s a Cretan and has traveled widely. Right now he’s escaped from a Thesprotian ship and has taken refuge at my station, so I’m putting him in your hands. Do whatever you think best with him, but remember he’s your suppliant.”

“I’m very troubled by what you’ve told me,” said Telemachus. “How can I take this stranger into my house? I’m still young and not strong enough to defend myself if anyone attacks me. My mother can’t decide whether to stay where she is and look after the house out of respect for public opinion and her husband’s memory, or whether it’s time to choose the best of her suitors—the one who’ll make her the most generous offer. Still, since the stranger has come to your station, I’ll provide him with a good cloak and shirt, a sword and sandals, and send him wherever he wants to go. Or if you prefer, you can keep him here at the station, and I’ll send clothes and food so he won’t be a burden on you and your men. But I won’t let him go near the suitors—they’re very insolent and would surely mistreat him in a way that would pain me greatly. No matter how brave a man is, he can’t fight against so many, for they’d overpower him.”

Then Odysseus said, “Sir, it’s right that I should speak up. I’m deeply shocked by what you’ve said about how insolently the suitors are behaving even with a man like you present. Tell me, do you submit to this treatment quietly, or has some god turned your people against you? Can’t you count on your brothers for support—for those are the ones a man looks to for help, no matter how serious his quarrel? I wish I were as young as you and in my present frame of mind. If I were Odysseus’s son, or indeed Odysseus himself, I’d rather have someone cut off my head than not go to that house and destroy every one of those men. If I stood alone against so many, I’d rather die fighting in my own house than witness such disgraceful scenes day after day: strangers brutally mistreated, men dragging the serving women around the house in an unseemly way, wine drawn recklessly, and bread squandered pointlessly for an end that will never come.”

Telemachus answered, “I’ll tell you the whole truth. There’s no hostility between me and my people, nor can I complain about brothers who might support me in any quarrel. Zeus has made us a line of only sons. Laertes was Arceisius’s only son, and Odysseus was Laertes’s only son. I’m Odysseus’s only son, left behind when he went away, so I’ve never been any help to him. That’s why my house is overrun with countless marauders. All the chiefs from the neighboring islands—Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus—as well as all the leading men of Ithaca itself are devouring my household under the pretense of courting my mother. She won’t flatly refuse to remarry, but she won’t bring the matter to an end either, so they’re destroying my estate and will soon destroy me as well. The outcome, however, rests with heaven. But you, old friend Eumaeus, go at once and tell Penelope that I’m safe and have returned from Pylos. Tell her alone, then come back here without letting anyone else know, for many are plotting against me.”

“I understand and will obey,” replied Eumaeus. “You need say no more. But since I’m going that way, should I also let poor Laertes know you’ve returned? He used to oversee the farm work despite his bitter grief over Odysseus, and would eat and drink normally with his servants. But they tell me that since the day you left for Pylos, he’s neither eaten nor drunk properly, nor does he tend his farm, but sits weeping and wasting the flesh off his bones.”

“That’s unfortunate,” answered Telemachus, “and I’m sorry for him, but we must leave him alone for now. If people could have everything they wanted, the first thing I’d choose would be my father’s return. But go and deliver your message, then hurry back without making a detour to tell Laertes. Have my mother send one of her women secretly with the news right away—let him hear it from her.”

So he urged the swineherd. Eumaeus put on his sandals and set off for town. Athena watched him leave the station, then approached in the form of a woman—beautiful, tall, and wise. She stood by the entrance, revealing herself to Odysseus, but Telemachus couldn’t see her and didn’t know she was there, for the gods don’t show themselves to everyone. Odysseus saw her, as did the dogs, who didn’t bark but whimpered and slunk away to the far side of the yard. She nodded and signaled to Odysseus with her eyebrows, so he left the hut and stood before her outside the main wall of the courtyard. Then she said:

“Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, it’s time to tell your son the truth. Don’t keep him in the dark any longer, but make your plans for destroying the suitors, then head for town. I won’t be long in joining you, for I too am eager for battle.”

As she spoke, she touched him with her golden wand. First she draped a clean shirt and cloak over his shoulders, then made him younger and more impressive in appearance. She restored his color, filled out his cheeks, and let his beard become dark again. Then she departed, and Odysseus returned to the hut. His son was amazed when he saw him and looked away, fearing he might be gazing upon a god.

“Stranger,” he said, “how suddenly you’ve changed from what you were just moments ago! You’re dressed differently and your color is not the same. Are you one of the gods who live in heaven? If so, be kind to me until I can make proper sacrifices and offerings of worked gold. Have mercy on me.”
Odysseus replied, “I’m no god—why do you mistake me for one? I am your father, for whose sake you grieve and suffer so much at the hands of lawless men.”
As he spoke, he kissed his son, and a tear fell from his cheek to the ground, for he had held back all tears until now. But Telemachus still couldn’t believe it was his father, and said:

“You’re not my father, but some god is deceiving me with false hopes so I’ll grieve even more later. No mortal man could do what you’ve just done—make himself old and young in an instant—unless a god were helping him. A moment ago you were old and dressed in rags, and now you look like a god come down from heaven.”

Odysseus answered, “Telemachus, you shouldn’t be so amazed that I’m really here. There is no other Odysseus to come after this one. Such as I am, it is I who, after long wandering and great hardship, have come home in the twentieth year to my own country. What amazes you is the work of the formidable goddess Athena, who does with me whatever she wishes, for she can do anything. One moment she makes me look like a beggar, the next I’m a young man in fine clothes. It’s easy for the gods who live in heaven to make any man appear rich or poor.”

As he spoke, he sat down, and Telemachus threw his arms around his father and wept. They were both so moved that they cried aloud like eagles or vultures with hooked claws whose half-fledged young have been stolen by farmers. They wept so pitifully that the sun would have set on their tears if Telemachus hadn’t suddenly asked, “In what ship, my dear father, did your crew bring you to Ithaca? And what people did they say they were?—for you can’t have come here by land.”

“I’ll tell you the truth, my son,” replied Odysseus. “The Phaeacians brought me here. They’re great sailors who escort anyone who reaches their shores. They carried me across the sea while I slept and landed me in Ithaca, giving me many gifts of bronze, gold, and clothing. By heaven’s grace, these are hidden in a cave, and I’ve come here on Athena’s advice so we can plan how to kill our enemies. First, give me a list of the suitors and their number, so I may learn who they are and how many. Then I can turn the matter over in my mind and see whether we two can fight them all ourselves, or if we need to find others to help us.”

Telemachus answered, “Father, I’ve always heard of your fame both in battle and in council, but what you’re suggesting is enormous—I’m awed just thinking about it. Two men can’t fight many brave ones. There aren’t just ten suitors, or even twenty, but many times that. Listen to their numbers: fifty-two chosen young men from Dulichium with six servants; twenty-four from Same; twenty young Achaeans from Zacynthus; and twelve from Ithaca itself, all well-born. They have with them a servant named Medon, a bard, and two carvers. If we face such numbers, you may bitterly regret your coming and your revenge. See if you can think of someone willing to help us.”
“Listen to me,” replied Odysseus, “and consider whether Athena and her father Zeus might be sufficient, or if I should try to find someone else as well.”
“Those you’ve named,” answered Telemachus, “are a good pair of allies. Though they dwell high among the clouds, they have power over both gods and mortals.”

“These two,” continued Odysseus, “won’t stay out of the fight long when the suitors and we clash in my house. Now, go home early tomorrow morning and mingle with the suitors as before. Later, the swineherd will bring me to the city disguised as a wretched old beggar. If you see them mistreating me, steel your heart against my suffering. Even if they drag me from the house by my feet or throw things at me, just watch and do nothing except gently try to make them behave more reasonably. But they won’t listen to you, for their day of reckoning is at hand. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—when Athena puts it in my mind, I’ll nod to you, and when you see me do this, gather all the weapons in the house and hide them in the strong storeroom. When the suitors ask why you’re removing them, make some excuse—say you’ve taken them away from the smoke, since they’re no longer what they were when Odysseus left, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you’re afraid Zeus might make them quarrel over their wine and harm each other, which would disgrace both the feast and the courtship, for the sight of weapons sometimes tempts people to use them. But leave a sword and spear each for you and me, and a couple of oxhide shields so we can grab them at any moment. Zeus and Athena will soon quiet these people. There’s also another matter: if you’re truly my son and my blood runs in your veins, let no one know that Odysseus is in the house—not Laertes, not the swineherd, not any of the servants, not even Penelope herself. Let just you and me test the women, and let’s also try some of the male servants to see who’s on our side and who’s against us.”

“Father,” replied Telemachus, “you’ll come to know me in time, and when you do, you’ll find I can keep your secrets. But I don’t think the plan you suggest will work well for either of us. Consider this: it will take us a long time to go around to all the farms and test the men, and meanwhile the suitors will be wasting your estate with impunity and without remorse. By all means test the women to see who are disloyal and who are innocent, but I’m not in favor of going around testing the men. We can deal with that later, if you really have some sign from Zeus that he’ll support you.”

While they talked, the ship that had brought Telemachus and his crew from Pylos reached the town of Ithaca. When they entered the harbor, they pulled the ship onto land. Their servants took their armor, and they left all the gifts at Clytius’s house. Then they sent a messenger to tell Penelope that Telemachus had gone to the country but had sent the ship to town to keep her from worrying. This messenger and Eumaeus happened to meet while both were on the same errand of informing Penelope. When they reached the house, the messenger stood up and announced to the queen in front of the waiting women, “Your son, my lady, has returned from Pylos.” But Eumaeus went directly to Penelope and privately told her everything her son had instructed him to say. After delivering his message, he left the house and grounds and returned to his pigs.

The suitors were surprised and angry at what had happened, so they went outside the great wall surrounding the outer court and held a council near the main gate. Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke first.

“My friends,” he said, “this voyage of Telemachus’s is a very serious matter. We were sure it would come to nothing. Now let’s launch a ship and gather a crew to send after the others, telling them to return as quickly as possible.”

He had barely finished speaking when Amphinomus turned and saw the ship in the harbor with the crew lowering the sails and stowing their oars. He laughed and said to the others, “We don’t need to send any message—they’re already here. Some god must have warned them, or they saw the ship pass and couldn’t catch up.”

At this they rose and went to the waterside. The crew pulled the ship ashore, their servants took their armor, and they all went up to the assembly place, not allowing anyone old or young to sit with them. Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke first.

“Good heavens,” he said, “see how the gods have saved this man from destruction! We kept scouts posted on the headlands all day, and when the sun set we didn’t go ashore to sleep but waited in the ship all night until morning, hoping to capture and kill him. But some god has brought him home despite us. Let’s figure out how to finish him off. He must not escape us—our plan is never likely to succeed while he’s alive, for he’s very clever, and public opinion isn’t entirely on our side. We must act quickly before he can call the Achaeans to assembly. He’ll waste no time doing so, for he’ll be furious with us and will tell everyone how we plotted to kill him but failed. The people won’t like this when they learn of it. We must make sure they don’t harm us or drive us from our own country into exile. Let’s try to catch him either on his farm away from town or on the road here. Then we can divide his property among ourselves and let his mother and whoever marries her keep the house. If this doesn’t appeal to you and you want Telemachus to live and keep his father’s property, then we shouldn’t gather here eating up his goods this way, but should make our offers to Penelope each from his own house. She can marry whoever offers the most for her and whose lot it is to win her.”

They all remained silent until Amphinomus rose to speak. He was the son of Nisus, who was King Aretias’s son, and he was the leading suitor from the wheat-growing, well-pastured island of Dulichium. His conversation pleased Penelope more than that of any other suitor, for he was a man of good character. “My friends,” he said, speaking to them plainly and in all honesty, “I’m not in favor of killing Telemachus. It’s a heinous thing to kill someone of noble blood. Let’s first consult the gods, and if Zeus’s oracles advise it, I’ll help kill him myself and urge everyone else to do so. But if they discourage us, I say we should hold back.”
His words pleased them, so they rose immediately and went to Odysseus’s house, where they took their usual seats.

Then Penelope decided to show herself to the suitors. She knew of the plot against Telemachus, for the servant Medon had overheard their plans and told her. So she went down to the courtyard with her maids, and when she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the gallery, holding a veil before her face, and rebuked Antinous:

“Antinous, you insolent and wicked schemer, they say you’re the best speaker and counselor of any man your age in Ithaca, but you’re nothing of the sort. Madman, why do you try to bring about Telemachus’s death, showing no respect for suppliants, whose witness is Zeus himself? It’s wrong for you to plot against each other this way. Don’t you remember how your father fled to this house in fear of the people, who were enraged at him for joining Taphian pirates and raiding the Thesprotians, who were at peace with us? They wanted to tear him apart and devour everything he owned, but Odysseus restrained them despite their fury. Now you’re consuming his property without paying for it, and you break my heart by courting his wife and trying to kill his son. Stop this behavior and make the others stop too.”

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered, “Take heart, Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, and don’t worry about these matters. The man isn’t yet born, and never will be, who will lay hands on your son Telemachus while I still live to see the light of day. I tell you—and it will surely happen—that my spear will be red with that man’s blood, for many times Odysseus took me on his knees, put wine to my lips, and placed meat in my hands. Therefore Telemachus is my dearest friend, and he has nothing to fear from us suitors. Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it.” He said this to calm her, but he was actually plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband until Athena brought sleep to her eyes. In the evening Eumaeus returned to Odysseus and his son, who had just sacrificed a year-old pig and were preparing supper together. Athena came to Odysseus, struck him with her wand to make him look like an old man again, and dressed him in his ragged clothes, fearing the swineherd might recognize him and fail to keep the secret by telling Penelope.
Telemachus spoke first. “So you’re back, Eumaeus,” he said. “What’s the news from town? Have the suitors returned, or are they still waiting somewhere to ambush me on my way home?”

“I didn’t think to ask about that when I was in town,” replied Eumaeus. “I thought I’d deliver my message and get back as quickly as possible. I met a messenger sent by those who sailed with you to Pylos, and he was first to tell your mother the news. But I can tell you what I saw with my own eyes: I had just reached the crest of Hermes’s hill above the town when I saw a ship entering the harbor with many men aboard. They had numerous shields and spears, and I thought it was the suitors, but I can’t be certain.”
Hearing this, Telemachus smiled at his father, taking care that Eumaeus couldn’t see him.

When they had finished their work and the meal was ready, they ate, and everyone had a full portion so all were satisfied. As soon as they had eaten and drunk enough, they lay down to rest and enjoyed the boon of sleep.
